To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the histamine releasing factor (HRF), a protein that induces histamine release from mast cells and basophils, is conserved in ticks and is a potential candidate for a vaccine to prevent tick infestation.
we have characterized four tick HRF homologies that share 91-98% sequence similarity with the DVHRF and that these proteins are expressed in all life stages of the tick.
we identified and characterized a histamine release factor homolog in ticks, which is a potential vaccine target antigen for multiple tick species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and biological characterization of tick HRF homology and their role(s) in tick-host interactions.
the molecular and biological analysis of tick HRF homology, which has been shown to play a critical role in the pathophysiology of allergic reactions in vertebrates.
identifying and characterizing tick salivary proteins that modulate vertebrate immune response and are involved in tick-host interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tick HRFs are highly conserved, ubiquitously expressed in tick tissues and developmentally unregulated, but not functionally conserved.
the HRF gene family is conserved in ticks and is ubiquitously expressed in all life stages.
DVHRF and orthologs are members of the TCTP protein family and are highly conserved across the Ixodid tick species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have cloned and characterized the cDNA of a histamine releasing factor from D. varibilis and have identified orthologs of this cDNA in other tick species, and have shown that the protein encoded is a secreted protein that is expressed in all tick developmental stages.
we have identified a novel family of HRFs in ticks that are expressed ubiquitously and may have a role in tick-host interaction.
the tick HRF gene family is conserved among all tick species tested, is expressed at the larval stage and is ubiquitously expressed in all developmental stages of the tick.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have shown that the tick HRF family is conserved among the three most important tick vectors of disease in the United States, the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanu), the American dog tick (Dermacentor variablis) and the Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacenter andersoni) and the Southern cattle tick (Boophilus microplus).
tick histamine release factor proteins are conserved and ubiquitously expressed in ticks, which make them ideal targets for development of novel vaccines and other tick control strategies.
the tick histamine release factor is a potential candidate for a vaccine to prevent tick infestation.
